scenes.heading: Goroutines
scenes.narration: Let's dig into goroutines, the lightweight threads of execution that make Go's concurrency model so cheap and so powerful.

scenes.heading: Why goroutines are cheap
items: Started by writing `go` before any function call
Managed by the Go runtime, not the OS
scenes.narration: Writing go in front of a function call launches a goroutine: a function that runs concurrently in the same address space. The runtime, not the operating system, schedules them, and each starts with a tiny two-kilobyte stack that grows on demand. That is why a single program can happily run hundreds of thousands of them.

scenes.heading: Lifecycle of `go worker()`
steps: Enqueue a new goroutine on a P
Scheduler runs it when a thread is free
Block, park, and switch to another
scenes.narration: When you launch a goroutine, Go evaluates the function and its arguments immediately, then places a new goroutine on a processor's run queue. Control returns to the caller right away — it does not wait. The GMP scheduler multiplexes many goroutines onto a few OS threads, and when one blocks on a channel or a syscall it parks it and runs another, keeping threads busy.

scenes.heading: Launch and wait with a WaitGroup
scenes.narration: Goroutines need coordination, and a sync.WaitGroup is the standard tool. We call Add before the go statement, each worker defers Done, and Wait blocks until the counter returns to zero. Passing i as an argument gives each goroutine its own copy, avoiding the classic loop-variable capture bug. Without the Wait, main could return and the whole program would exit before the workers ever ran.

scenes.text: A goroutine blocked forever with no exit path is a leak — always give it a way to return.
scenes.narration: The biggest reliability risk is a goroutine leak: a goroutine blocked forever on a channel with no counterpart or with no cancellation. It never returns, holding its stack. Always give every goroutine a clear exit — a return, a closed channel, or context cancellation.

scenes.text: Cheap concurrency, but bound it: use pools, WaitGroups, context, and the -race detector.
scenes.narration: Goroutines make high concurrency almost free, but production code bounds them with worker pools, coordinates completion with WaitGroups and context, and runs tests with the race detector to catch unsynchronized shared state.
